title: Douglas Hofstadter: Analogy as the Core of Cognition [video]
author: tosh
tldr: An older talk by Douglas Hofstadter arguing that analogy-making is not a high-level reasoning trick but the basic act of thought, running from perception up to how we form categories in the first place.
articleNote: Video; not summarized. The tldr is pieced together from the HN thread, and the digest covers the discussion.

comments.overview: A warm, wide-ranging thread that mostly used the talk as a jumping-off point, since few commenters said they had watched it. The longest exchange asked whether analogy or prediction better describes what brains do. The rest split between Hofstadter's mixed record against modern LLMs and a meta-argument over whether analogies help or hurt when you argue with someone.

themes.title: Analogy or prediction as the brain's core job
themes.synthesis: HarHarVeryFunny ran a long debate claiming the brain is built for prediction. The cortex's repeating six-layer circuit sends top-down predictions to meet sensory input, prediction is what survival demands, and calling it analogy adds a dense book where one sentence would do. killerstorm answered that "generalization" is vague, and that analogy names a sharper mechanism, comparing things along a chosen feature rather than by raw similarity. A parent's story of a 6-month-old spotting Winnie the Pooh on a towel served as evidence for both sides.

quotes.author: HarHarVeryFunny
quotes.text: So, my question for Hofstader, or you, would be given that the brain seems to be literally built for prediction, then what is to be gained by regarding this as analogy making instead? Is there any evidence for this?

quotes.author: killerstorm
quotes.text: Analogy-making points to more specific mechanism: ability to identify features within representations, and modulating associative lookup using those features. I.e. it's not as simple as D(x, y) i.e. distance between embeddings, but something like D(f(x), f(y)) where f projects representation to a specific feature space.

themes.title: Hofstadter's ideas next to LLMs
themes.synthesis: Several commenters pointed out that embedding spaces already do analogy, word2vec's king-and-queen arithmetic being the famous case, and that an autoregressive model feeding its own output back in looks like a strange loop. Others traced Hofstadter's own shift: a long-time skeptic who, by 2023, said LLMs made him feel "diminished" while still calling their intelligence empty. One commenter read that as heartbreak, not dismissal. antonvs asked why an LLM's intelligence counts as empty when many humans also stop learning after their early years. A side thread over Scott Aaronson's recent post questioned whether Hofstadter ever claimed cognition needs self-reference, or only consciousness.

quotes.author: jameshart
quotes.text: I’m confused why there seems to be a dismissal of the most basic ‘strange loop’ of the LLM - the fact that it’s evaluating a context to choose the next word, then reevaluating in a context where that word has been appended.

quotes.author: calebkaiser
quotes.text: When he's describing modern systems as "empty intelligence", I think there's a little bit of heartbreak in his perspective, because he sees them as fundamentally different from humans in a way that leaves the part he loves--the "I" in the loop--out of the equation.

themes.title: Analogies explain well and persuade badly
themes.synthesis: A remark that sharing an analogy is the fastest way to lose an argument started a long branch. Terr_ said an analogy hands a hostile listener a second set of claims to attack. dofm said a hole in an analogy is a given and tells you nothing. jt2190 took the opposite line and asked people to say what a thing is, not what it is like. Others noted that the complaint itself was built on spatial metaphors like "losing" an argument, which is close to Hofstadter's point.

quotes.author: Terr_
quotes.text: I think that's just because every analogy gives an entire "second front" of ideas for a hostile recipient to find a "flaw", when they ignore the intended boundary between the stuff that does/doesn't matter to the analogy.

quotes.author: dofm
quotes.text: The fact of a hole in an analogy is not in itself information. Of course there's a hole.

themes.title: When a far-reaching analogy earns its keep
themes.synthesis: patcon's claim that protein folding and storytelling share structure drew a warning from gilleain, who recalled a 1960s program that "discovered" the atom-as-solar-system analogy, a mapping that teaches little about either. patcon, trained in biochemistry, replied with concrete work: treating stories as one-dimensional chains that fold into a mental model, and porting folding-analysis methods to audience reaction data. Biologists, he said, improved their own tools after seeing his. gilleain's caution held for analogies between distant systems, and patcon conceded the value lies mostly in moving methods across domains.

quotes.author: gilleain
quotes.text: reasoning through analogy is fun and can be useful, it is just limited in what it can do, especially the further apart the systems are.

quotes.author: patcon
quotes.text: Someone could get to my conclusions another way, but the metaphors are my cheat codes to arrive there early :)

themes.title: Older roots of the idea
themes.synthesis: Commenters placed the thesis in a longer line: Nietzsche on the drive to form metaphors, and above all George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By, which several recommended as the better book on the subject. goatlover noted that if metaphors shape thought this much, an alien species with a different body might think in ways hard to decode. A side story about the Pioneer plaque's arrow, a hunting symbol aliens might not read, made the same point.

quotes.author: vonnik
quotes.text: Every category and noun is an analogy uniting things unlike in at least some details. We don’t even see most analogies, because they are more common than air and just as necessary.

comments.consensus: Analogy runs deep in how people think and talk, and modern embedding-based models do something that looks a lot like it. Hofstadter's books, Gödel, Escher, Bach and I Am a Strange Loop in particular, changed how many readers think.
comments.dissent: Whether analogy is the mechanism of cognition or just a way to describe it. The prediction camp argued that brain anatomy and evolution point to prediction, with analogy as a byproduct, and that a theory needing that many examples has not shown its claim.

contrarian.author: HarHarVeryFunny
contrarian.text: All we get in this video is a rambling set of example analogies.
contrarian.why: The only commenter who said he watched the talk reports that it piles up examples without making the case, the same complaint reviewers made about Surfaces and Essences, while most of the thread praised Hofstadter on reputation.
